questions.title: Why must the court view evidence 'in the light most favorable to the verdict' when reversing a JMOL denial?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to understand the procedural standard for JMOL review here. The opinion says the court should reverse only if 'viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict, the evidence points so strongly and overwhelmingly in favor of one party that the court believes that reasonable jurors could not arrive at any contrary conclusion.' Can someone explain how this extreme standard differs from a normal 'substantial evidence' review of jury findings, and why it's so hard to reverse a jury verdict under this standard? Also, why does the court apply Fifth Circuit law instead of Fed. Cir. law here?

questions.title: How does expert testimony that is 'self-contradictory' fail to support a jury verdict under the substantial evidence standard?
questions.question_body: In section II.A regarding the '134 patent, the Federal Circuit reverses the jury verdict because Dr. Wells' testimony was 'confusing and unclear' and 'self-contradictory.' The court says Finesse 'rested its case on an expert's self-contradictory testimony.' Could someone walk me through exactly why Dr. Wells' statements about x1, x2, the DL(TX) reference, and the modeled PIM path being contradictory? How would this same reasoning apply if the expert had tried to explain their testimony differently? And why is contradictory testimony fatal when the expert witness is what establishes the factual basis for infringement?

questions.title: Does amending patent claims to overcome a prior art rejection constitute 'surrender of claim scope' over products that would qualify for infringement?
questions.question_body: For the '775 patent, the Federal Circuit says Finesse 'did not surrender claim scope over products, like the accused radios, with two unique input signals.' The opinion cites Cont'l Circuits LLC v. Intel Corp. about what raises the level to 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal. Can someone explain what actually constitutes 'claim scope surrender' in patent prosecution? When is an amendment clear enough to surrender over particular claims/products? And why did the court conclude that amending from 'two or three signals' to just 'three signals' didn't forcefully disavow products using two signals as separate inputs?

questions.title: What is the effect of vacating a damages award when the infringement verdict is reversed on appeal?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit reverses the noninfringement JMOL for both the '134 and '775 patents and then vacates the damages award. I understand that without an infringement finding, there can be no damages award. But can someone explain the procedural implications here - does vacating the damages award mean the case goes back for retrial on infringement only, or does it also mean the case goes back for a complete new trial? Also, if the jury awarded 'lump-sum damages for the remaining life of the patents,' how does reversal of infringement findings affect that calculation, and what happens to the $166 million award?

questions.title: How does professional construction of claim terms limit what the Supreme Court says 'cannot be surrendered'?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that 'the district court construed 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' to be 'separately identifiable,' but not 'unique.' This seems to be the claim construction that determines whether the accused device could infringe. Can someone explain how district court claim construction becomes part of the legal issue for standard of review purposes at different stages of the appeal? And how does this claim construction - once established - stay relevant even when the testimony moving forward questions whether each limitation was actually met?

questions.title: Why does the absence of a mapping from Nokia documents to claim limitations invalidate the infringement evidence?
questions.question_body: For the '775 patent, Dr. Wells relied on a Nokia document to show the accused radios performed the claimed multiplications. The Federal Circuit says 'no reasonable jury could have found that the accused radios perform the seven claimed multiplications.' The court states the document 'does not disclose multiplying x1 and x2, but their complex conjugate and modulus.' Can someone explain why the failure to provide a clear mapping from the technical document to the claim language is dispositive for an infringement finding? Is this a matter of evidence sufficiency, or is it about whether the elements are actually present, or something else?

questions.title: What is the difference between 'substantial evidence' review for factual findings versus 'clear error' review for district court's claim construction?
questions.question_body: The standard paragraph at the beginning of the Discussion section reviews four different standards: (1) JMOL denial for the Fifth Circuit, (2) infringement findings for substantial evidence, (3) underlying factual findings for clear error, (4) claim construction de novo. Can someone help me understand why these different standards apply at different levels, and how they relate to the overall appeal outcome? Also, if claim construction is reviewed 'de novo,' why did the district court's claim construction matter significantly if they're going to review it de novo on appeal?
